'''Victor Ninov''' ({{langx|bg|Виктор Нинов}}; born 27 June 1959) is a Bulgarian physicist and former researcher who worked primarily in creating [[superheavy element]]s.  He is known for the co-discoveries of elements 110, 111, and 112 ([[darmstadtium]], [[roentgenium]], and [[copernicium]], respectively).<ref name=":1"/> 
Ninov also claimed the creation of elements [[livermorium|116]] and [[oganesson|118]] (now livermorium and oganesson);<ref name=":8" /><ref name="NYT20021015" /> however, an investigation conducted by the [[University of California, Berkeley]] concluded that he had falsified the evidence. The repercussions of the affair had an impact on the guidelines of conduct for several research institutions.

== Early life ==
Victor Ninov was born in [[People's Republic of Bulgaria|Bulgaria]] in 1959.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Fontani |first1=Marco |chapter=The Obsession of Physicists with the Frontier: The Case of Ausonium and Hesperium, Littorium and Mussolinium |date=2014-11-20 |chapter-url=https://academic.oup.com/book/40694/chapter/348413219 |title=The Lost Elements |access-date=2023-11-13 |publisher=Oxford University Press |language=en |doi=10.1093/oso/9780199383344.003.0016 |isbn=978-0-19-938334-4 |last2=Costa |first2=Mariagrazia |last3=Orna |first3=Mary Virginia|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> He grew up in the capital city of [[Sofia]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite news |last=Sauro |first=Tony |date=23 July 2016 |title=Final assignment: Family, friends and colleagues help complete late Pacific professor's book |work=recordnet |url=https://www.recordnet.com/story/entertainment/books/2016/07/24/final-assignment-family-friends-colleagues/27441940007/ |url-access=limited |access-date=6 February 2023}}</ref> In the 1970s, when Ninov was a teenager, he and his family left for [[West Germany]],<ref name=":0">{{cite magazine |url=https://www.chronicle.com/article/Atomic-Lies/31825|title= Atomic Lies: How One Physicist May Have Cheated in the Race to Find New Elements|magazine=[[The Chronicle of Higher Education]]|date= 16 August 2002|first=Richard|last= Monastersky |access-date= 16 April 2019}}</ref> Shortly after the move, Victor's father went missing; he was found dead six months later in the Bulgarian foothills due to causes unknown.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Victor Ninov attended [[Technische Universität Darmstadt]] near [[Frankfurt|Frankfurt, Germany]].<ref name=":0"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Welcome to TU Darmstadt |trans-title=Darmstadt University of Technology |url=https://www.tu-darmstadt.de/universitaet/index.en.jsp |access-date=23 April 2019 |website=Technische Universität Darmstadt |language=en}}</ref> He distinguished himself as a very capable physicist: he was particularly good at building scientific instruments and coding analysis programs for them.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last=Dalton |first=Rex |date=18 July 2002 |title=California lab fires physicist over retracted finding |journal=Nature |volume=418 |page=261 |bibcode=2002Natur.418..261D |doi=10.1038/418261b |pmid=12124581 |doi-access=free |number=6895}}</ref>

He was hired by the nearby German research center [[GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research|GSI]] (''Helmholtzzentrum für Schwerionenforschung''), where he completed his doctorate and pursued postdoctoral work creating new elements.<ref name=":0"/><ref>{{Cite web |last=GSI Helmholtzzentrum für Schwerionenforschung |date=17 January 2012 |title=GSI - About us |url=https://www.gsi.de/en/about_us?nr=754 |access-date=23 April 2019 |website=gsi.de |language=en}}</ref>

For his expertise, he was given sole control of the computer analysis program.<ref name=":0" /> Here, he became a rising star by co-discovering [[darmstadtium]] (element 110), [[roentgenium]] (element 111), and [[copernicium]] (element 112) by smashing ion beams into heavy elements using GSI's [[UNILAC]] (a type of [[particle accelerator]]) and analyzing the debris.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1"/> Though an investigation later determined that the discovery of elements 110 and 112 included samples fabricated by Ninov, the overall results were validated on further examination, rendering his co-discovery legitimate.<ref name=":1" /><ref name="Rg27202Ho01">{{Cite journal |last1=Hofmann |first1=S. |last2=Heßberger |first2=F. P. |last3=Ackermann |first3=D. |last4=Münzenberg |first4=G. |last5=Antalic |first5=S. |last6=Cagarda |first6=P. |last7=Kindler |first7=B. |last8=Kojouharova |first8=J. |last9=Leino |first9=M. |last10=Lommel |first10=B. |last11=Mann |first11=R. |last12=Popeko |first12=A.G. |last13=Reshitko |first13=S. |last14=Śaro |first14=S. |last15=Uusitalo |first15=J. |display-authors=2 |date=1 July 2002 |title=New results on elements 111 and 112 |journal=The European Physical Journal A |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=147–157 |bibcode=2002EPJA...14..147H |doi=10.1140/epja/i2001-10119-x |last16=Yeremin |first16=A.V. |s2cid=8773326}}</ref> These discoveries were facilitated by Ninov's addition of a gas separator to the particle accelerator to help filter out everything but the heavy elements they were looking for.

After working at [[Stanford University]], Ninov<ref name=":3"/> was hired by [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] (LBNL) in 1996 as a world class expert in particle accelerator debris sensors and analysis programs.<ref name=":0" />

== Fraud investigation ==
While working at LBNL, Ninov and his team pursued a hypothesis by [[Robert Smolańczuk]], then a visiting fellow from Poland on a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright]] scholarship,{{Citation needed|date=September 2024}} that element 118 could be formed at relatively low energies by smashing [[Isotopes of krypton|<sup>86</sup>Kr]] and [[Isotopes of lead|<sup>208</sup>Pb]] isotopes together.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Seife |first=Charles |date=19 July 2002 |title=Heavy-element fizzle laid to falsified data. (Heavy-Ion Physics) |work=Science |url=https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.297.5580.313 |doi=10.1126/science.297.5580.313}}</ref><ref name=":0"/> This hypothesis was dubbed "Robert's magic recipe", and it was highly controversial at the time.{{Citation needed|date=September 2024}} Ninov initially doubted the hypothesis he was pursuing; he is quoted as saying, "We didn't know how many orders of magnitude he [Smolańczuk] was wrong".<ref name=":0" />

As in some earlier research projects, Ninov had exclusive control of the data analysis program (LBNL's was called GOOSY) since he was the only team member who knew how to use it.<ref name=":0" /> In 1999, Ninov and his team reported sightings of element 118, almost exactly as in Smolańczuk's hypothesis, and a decay chain that also produced element 116.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4">{{cite journal |last=Schwarzschild |first=Bertram |date=September 2002 |title=Lawrence Berkeley Lab concludes that evidence of element 118 was a fabrication |journal=Physics Today |volume=55 |page=15– |bibcode=2002PhT....55i..15S |doi=10.1063/1.1522199 |doi-access=free |number=9}}</ref><ref name=":1"/><ref name=":2" /> However, other laboratories were unable to reproduce the results.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=Weiss|first=P|date=July 2002|title=Heavy Suspicion|url=http://web.b.ebscohost.com.cod.idm.oclc.org/ehost/detail/detail?vid=3&sid=a5d68c77-44d8-4e6c-acd5-3b0d7325afce%40pdc-v-sessmgr05&bdata=JnNpdGU9ZWhvc3QtbGl2ZSZzY29wZT1zaXRl#AN=7015529&db=a9h|journal=Science News|volume=162|pages=2|via=Academic Search Complete}}</ref>

Eager to prove their discovery, the team double-checked their instruments, and tried again.<ref name=":0"/> One more sighting was made by Ninov, but it was dismissed by a colleague and a formal investigation was launched.<ref name=":0" /> The original element 118 data were independently analysed. In the original binary data, there was no indication of the presence of element 118 or 116.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4"/><ref name=":1"/><ref name=":2"/><ref name=":5"/> The investigation eventually concluded that Ninov had fabricated the data.<ref name=":5" />

Ninov, who had been placed on leave for the investigation, was dismissed.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> The rest of Ninov's team officially retracted their claims in 2002.<ref name=":4" /> There was also an investigation conducted into Ninov's previous unsupervised science at GSI; it was found that "two sightings were spuriously created" (one of element 110 and another of element 112).<ref name=":1" /><ref name="Rg27202Ho01"/> However these false sightings were found amongst a large amount of real data that still supported his co-discoveries of elements 110 and 112.<ref name=":1" /> The GSI investigation concluded that the discovery of those elements was legitimate.<ref name=":1" />

The superheavy elements 116 and 118 were eventually discovered and verified in the [[Joint Institute for Nuclear Research]] in [[Dubna|Dubna, Russia]] from 2000 to 2002.<ref name=":5" /> These elements were named [[livermorium]] and [[oganesson]] respectively.<ref name=":8">{{cite journal|last=Ninov|first=Viktor|date=1999|title=Observation of Superheavy Nuclei Produced in the Reaction of <sup>86</sup>Kr with <sup>208</sup>Pb|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1233919|journal=[[Physical Review Letters]]|volume=83|issue=6|pages=1104–1107|bibcode=1999PhRvL..83.1104N|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.83.1104}}</ref><ref name="NYT20021015">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/10/15/science/at-lawrence-berkeley-physicists-say-a-colleague-took-them-for-a-ride.html?scp=2&sq=victor%20ninov&st=cse&pagewanted=1 |title=At Lawrence Berkeley, Physicists Say a Colleague Took Them for a Ride |work=The New York Times|date= 15 October 2002 |first= George |last=Johnson}}</ref> In 2010, some of the nuclides that were originally claimed as decay products of element 118 were truly synthesized at LBNL; the 2010 observations did not match the claimed 1999 data.<ref name="281Cn">
{{Cite news
 |author=Public Affairs Department
 |date=26 October 2010
 |title=Six New Isotopes of the Superheavy Elements Discovered: Moving Closer to Understanding the Island of Stability
 |url=https://newscenter.lbl.gov/news-releases/2010/10/26/six-new-isotopes
 |publisher=[[Berkeley Lab]]
 |access-date=2011-04-25
}}</ref> Ninov has continued to maintain that he was innocent.<ref name=":0"/>

===Impact on the scientific community===
The findings shocked the scientific community as Ninov had been a highly respected physicist.<ref name=":0"/> In fact, [[Albert Ghiorso]], a physicist who co-discovered 12 elements and a close collaborator of [[Glenn T. Seaborg|Glenn Seaborg]], once called Ninov "a younger version of himself". It was also troubling that so many co-authors of the LBNL's 1999 paper had been unaware that their discoveries were false.<ref name=":6">{{cite journal|last= Park|first= Robert L|title=Fraud in Science|journal=Social Research| volume= 75|number= 4|date= 2008|pages= 1135–1150 |doi= 10.1353/sor.2008.0010|url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/527631|s2cid= 141705050|url-access= subscription}}</ref> The affair resulted in stricter guidelines for coauthors, clarifying their roles and duties and requiring them to vouch for their contributions to published work.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/11/19/science/after-two-scandals-physics-group-expands-ethics-guidelines.html|title=After Two Scandals, Physics Group Expands Ethics Guidelines|last=Overbye|first=Dennis|date=19 November 2002|work=The New York Times|access-date=25 April 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

The [[American Physical Society]] called for increased ethical training and oversight at research institutions and sponsored educational efforts to make the scientific community more resilient to scientific fraud.<ref name=":7" /> Reports on the Ninov affair were released around the same time as the final report on the [[Jan Hendrik Schön|Schön affair]], another major incident of data falsification in physics, and this amplified its impact.<ref name=":7"/>

==Personal life==
His wife, Caroline Cox, a former history professor at University of the Pacific, died in 2014 of cancer. They were married for 23 years. Ninov had helped her finish her book, ''Boy Soldiers of the American Revolution'', and it was published posthumously. He pilots a four-seat plane, an [[Aero Commander]].<ref name=":3" />
